records.title: Continuous Low-Altitude Lunar Coverage Using Solar-Sail-Controlled Near-Circular Orbits
records.summary: Small satellites are increasingly tasked with ambitious missions in environments usually reserved for large, fuel-reliant spacecraft. Low Lunar Orbit (LLO) is particularly valuable for high-resolution imaging needed for landing site assessment and water ice observations; however, orbits at low altitudes (¡100 km) are inherently unstable due to lunar mascon perturbations and Earth’s third-body effects, and past missions required frequent propulsive maneuvers that restricted low-altitude imaging time to short periods. Without continuous station-keeping, satellites in this dynamic system typically impact the surface within weeks. Solar sails offer continuous, propellantless thrust and thus the potential for long-duration operations in LLO, but their accelerations are orders of magnitude smaller than the perturbations they must offset, and lunar eclipses regularly eliminate thrust for extended periods, during which uncontrolled eccentricity growth poses a threat to satellite survival. To overcome these challenges, this work adapts locally sub-optimal solar sail control frameworks for station-keeping in polar LLO by leveraging Gauss’s planetary equations to relate solar radiation pressure (SRP) acceleration to orbital element perturbations, defining an objective function as a weighted sum of orbital element deviations multiplied by their corresponding Gaussian terms. Maximizing this function identifies the required SRP acceleration vector— and thus the optimal sail attitude— while adaptive weights prioritize perilune preservation, minimize apolune growth, or adjust ω (argument of perilune). FreeFlyer simulations incorporating the LP165P lunar gravity model, Earth’s third-body effects, and SRP acceleration from a Solar Cruiser-sized sail (13 m 2 kg −1 ) show that a 25 km, nearly circular, polar orbit can be sustained for at least one year, even through repeated shadow cycles, with corrected eccentricity growth and natural 180 ◦ ω transfers that alternate the low-altitude ground track between hemispheres, enabling extended global low-altitude imaging coverage.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Debris Evolution from Spacecraft Fragmentation in Earth-Moon Distant Retrograde Orbits
records.summary: With the rapid surge in lunar exploration and the planned expansion of cislunar infrastructure, cislunar space has become a strategic focal point for global aerospace activities. This proliferation of spacecraft heightens the risk of fragmentation events, such as unintended explosions or orbital collisions which serve as the primary source of hazardous orbital debris. Given the potential threat these fragments pose to mission safety and long-term orbital sustainability, it is imperative to investigate their dynamical behavior within the Earth-Moon system. This study evaluates the dispersion of debris clouds following potential breakup events on Distant Retrograde Orbits (DROs) over a 30-day propagation period. The Circular Restricted Three-Body Problem (CR3BP) model is used to construct the reference orbits, while the NASA Standard Breakup Model is applied to simulate fragment generation at multiple locations along three DROs of varying sizes. These fragments are then propagated using the Bicircular Restricted Four-Body Problem (BCR4BP) for 30 days. To account for the variability of these events, multiple initial positions along each orbit are analyzed to capture a comprehensive range of post-explosion scenarios. Our analysis quantifies the fate of fragments within this window, specifically focusing on the escape mechanisms and the percentages of debris that either depart from the Earth-Moon gravitational sphere of influence or impact the lunar surface. Furthermore, we introduce an analytical approach to assess the potential collision risk to resident space objects operating within the vicinity of the parent orbit. The results provide insights into debris evolution and offer a foundation for developing safety guidelines for future cislunar activities.

records.title: Enhancing Risk-Informed Decision Making Through LLM-Based Concern Analysis in the Human Landing System Program
records.summary: The NASA Human Landing System (HLS) Program is a central component of the Artemis campaign, enabling crewed lunar surface missions and supporting long‑term exploration objectives. As part of NASA’s public–private development strategy, the program integrates Commercial Providers’ lander designs with NASA’s insight and oversight responsibilities to ensure crew safety, mission performance, and sustainable lunar operations. To manage the technical and programmatic uncertainties inherent to this effort, the HLS Program employs an Agency‑defined Risk Management framework built on Risk‑Informed Decision Making (RIDM) and Continuous Risk Management (CRM). A key element of this process is the identification and maturation of Office Concerns, which serve as early indicators of potential risks requiring additional definition before formal assessment. However, recognizing thematic similarity across numerous Concerns remains challenging due to variations in technical perspective and overlapping subject matter. This study evaluates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in grouping, comparing, and clarifying Office Concerns to enhance consistency and support timely maturation into program‑level risks. By converting concerns into embedding vectors, analyzing similarity relationships, and visualizing emerging themes, the approach provides a scalable method for identifying patterns. A hybrid methodology, integrating LLM‑based clustering with Microsoft Copilot‑generated thematic categorization, demonstrates improved repeatability, efficiency, and potential applicability across broader HLS risk and certification processes.

records.title: Establishing a proto-LTC with Two-Way Satellite Time Transfer (TWSTT) at the Moon
records.summary: This ECI project seeks to address these critical timing needs to develop a system capability for a “proto”- coordinated lunar time (LTC) scale and determine its empirical relationship with the standard terrestrial time scale. Complementary efforts are focused on defining an interoperable framework for communication, PNT, and auxiliary services in cislunar space (known as LunaNet) or advancing low TRL next generation highly stable clock technologies (such as the Spaceflight Compatible Optical Atomic Strontium Ion Clock, or OASIC). This proposed concept is focused on the development of a low small size, weight, and power (low SWaP) clock ensemble using flight-rated COTS parts to be deployed on the lunar surface, and the long-distance twoway satellite time transfer (TWSTT) procedure necessary for defining and tracing the lunar time relationship to UTC. This is a key technological effort because it will establish a feasible means to close the current gap in lunar timing service infrastructure in the next 3-5 years. Systems designed to obtain and distribute measurements of proper lunar time from the lunar surface are needed by lunar PNT systems such as LCRNS. The steady increase in missions going to the Moon will continue to strain the ground station infrastructure to meet cislunar missions’ needs for ranging, Doppler, and timing, when in view. The availability of a timing source providing a stable LTC reference to users on the lunar surface and in orbit can: 1) improve the navigation solutions of cislunar and lunar surface missions, when used as a source for the LunaNet PNT services, thereby unifying the distribution of a common lunar reference system commensurate with LTC; 2) reduce the timing burden on cislunar users by allowing them to use lower SWaP receivers, clocks, and processing power since the LTC time broadcast by the LunaNet Service Provider (LNSP) nodes are orbiting the same central body, are close by, and can more frequently provide time updates through the one-way broadcast; 3) serve as the foundation to establish a common time system for the Moon, analogous to International Atomic Time (TAI) or UTC on Earth. Benefits: The decades ahead will witness monumental advances in the exploration of cislunar space. Following the success of Artemis I and the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS), subsequent missions will return astronauts, robotic explorers, and science instruments to lunar orbit and the lunar surface, with the goal of establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon and vibrant lunar ecosystem in preparing for Mars. Critical to these endeavors will be establishing a time system at the Moon, to perform experiments of fundamental physics, testing predictions of relativity, and support a ...

records.title: Evaluation of image simulation open source solutions for simulation of synthetic images in lunar environment
records.summary: Synthetic image generation is one of the crucial input for planetary missions. It enables researchers and engineers to visualize planned planetary missions, test imaging systems and plan exploration activities in a virtual environment before actual deployment. Image simulation is essential for assessing landing sites, detecting hazards, and validating navigation systems in a missions. This study offers a detailed evaluation of various image simulation approaches for the lunar environment, with particular emphasis on the effects of different camera models and light illumination conditions on the quality of synthetic lunar images. These images are produced using real Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and terrain data derived from instruments such as Chandrayaan-2 Orbiter High Resolution Camera (OHRC) and NASA's Wide Angle Camera (WAC), and Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) instruments. This research aims to improve the reliability of synthetic imagery in supporting autonomous navigation and decision-making systems in lunar exploration. This work contributes to the development of more effective tools for generating important information for future lunar missions and enhances the understanding of the moon's surface environment.

records.title: Exosphere Modeling for Pole
records.summary: For FY26, the proposed study is to conduct theoretical analysis and supercomputer simulations to predict lunar surface charging observables for when the Moon is in the solar wind and Earth's magnetotail, taking into account extreme space weather conditions. Benefits: The expected outcome include observables such as spatial profiles of the electric potential, plasma density, and electron energy flux. These observables will serve to guide (1) the measurement requirements and instrument placement for GSFC's Plasma Observatory for Lunar Exploration (POLE) mission, and (2) the development of a pipeline of instruments to perform lunar south pole plasma/field measurements. The expected benefit is for NASA/GSFC to lead lunar south pole plasma measurements, addressing directly to the Moon Base Program Phase 1 and the Executive Order 14369 Ensuring American's Space ...

records.title: Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1: SCALPSS 1.1 Payload and Mission Overview
records.summary: The Stereo Cameras for Lunar Plume-Surface Studies (SCALPSS) 1.1 payload collected first-of-its-kind calibrated stereo imagery during the transit, descent, landing, and 14-day surface mission of the Firefly Aerospace Blue Ghost Mission 1 (BGM1) lander in early 2025. The payload, which was manifested on BGM1 in early 2021 and delivered to the provider in late 2022, included commercial off-the-shelf and “build-to-print” hardware with previous flight heritage. This included six cameras, which utilized three types of lenses optimized for both pre- and post-landing measurements with the stereo photogrammetry technique. The payload performed several image captures during lunar transit, including during a lunar orbit insertion burn and while in low-lunar orbit. During descent and landing on March 2nd, the payload acquired and transferred to the lander approximately 1800 images, which captured several key phenomena of interest to the plume-surface interaction topic. During the subsequent 14-day surface mission, several thousand additional images were collected and transferred to ground; these images were post-processed to produce high dynamic range images of the post-landing terrain as the lunar day progressed. The stereo photogrammetry technique is applied to the images to produce three-dimensional shape measurements of the lunar terrain, and is expected to provide an assessment of plume-induced erosion from the powered landing, which will inform modeling and predictive efforts for future landings at the Moon, Mars, and elsewhere.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: From Early Concepts to Lunar Hypertelescopes Roadmap for Next-Generation Optical Astronomy on the Moon
records.summary: Since the dawn of the Space Age, the Moon has been considered one of the most promising locations for astronomical observations. The absence of atmosphere, exceptional mechanical stability, access to the permanently shielded radio-quiet far side, and the possibility of constructing extremely large apertures have motivated numerous concepts for lunar observatories over the past six decades. Despite extensive studies conducted during the Apollo era, most proposed lunar astronomy projects remained unrealized due to technological limitations, shifting scientific priorities, and the high cost of sustained lunar operations. Today, renewed international interest in lunar exploration, combined with advances in robotics, autonomous systems, additive manufacturing, precision optics, and formation flying, is reopening the prospect of large-scale astronomical infrastructures on the Moon. In particular, lunar hypertelescope concepts offer the possibility of achieving unprecedented angular resolutions through diluted optical arrays spanning hundreds of meters to several kilometres. This paper reviews the historical evolution of lunar astronomy concepts, analyses the reasons behind previous failures, examines current technological developments, and proposes a roadmap toward future lunar hypertelescope facilities capable of transforming observational astronomy during the twenty-first century.

records.title: From Earth's Harshest Landscapes to Lunar Horizons: Engineering NEA Telescopes for Extreme Environments
records.summary: Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs) represent both a scientific opportunity and a potential threat to human civilization. While current survey programs have successfully detected most large NEAs, a significant observational gap remains for objects smaller than approximately 140 m, which can still produce regional-scale devastation. Ground-based surveys are intrinsically limited by atmospheric conditions, weather, and solar avoidance constraints, which leave a significant fraction of near-Sun objects difficult to detect. In particular, Earth-based observatories remain largely blind to objects approaching from the Sun-ward direction, reducing available warning times. Future lunar observatories offer a promising solution to this limitation. A telescope operating on the Moon could enable observations of regions inaccessible from Earth, provide enhanced sensitivity, and significantly improve early detection capabilities. However, the lunar environment imposes severe engineering constraints, including thermal cycling, dust contamination, radiation exposure, and autonomous operation requirements. We propose the AMAS(Atacama-Mongolia-Antarctica-Sahara) project, an international initiative using Earth's most extreme environments as analogue sites for future lunar astronomical facilities. By deploying and testing specialized NEA survey telescopes in these environments, key technologies for future lunar observatories can be validated under realistic operational conditions. This paper presents the scientific rationale, engineering challenges, site selection strategy, and long-term roadmap toward a global Earth-Moon network for planetary defense.

records.title: Harness Thermal Heat Loss Measurement for A Lunar Surface-Deployed LEMS Artemis III Payload
records.summary: The Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS) is an autonomous, survive-the-lunar-night seismic suite to be deployed on the Lunar surface by the Artemis III crew and designed to operate continuously for two years. It will see the extremes of the Lunar south pole thermal environment where surface temperatures range from -200°C to +20°C and where nighttime duration is at least 354 hours. Given power and mass constraints, the thermal system is limited to 2.5 Watts of heat during the lunar night. The electrical harnessing named the Signal and Power Passthrough (SAPP) was designed to minimize heat loss while meeting power and signal integrity requirements. To mitigate risk due to uncertainty associated with the harnessing materials, routing, and tie-downs, a flight-like thermal conductance test was performed to measure the heat loss. The test methodology, results, and model correlation are presented.

records.title: High-Power AM-CW Lunar Laser Ranging as a $μ$Hz SGWB Detector
records.summary: High-power amplitude-modulated continuous-wave lunar laser ranging (AM-CW LLR) is a stochastic-gravitational-wave-background (SGWB) experiment that measures GW-driven drift and diffusion of the Earth--Moon orbit. Its observable is the coherent phase of a GHz modulation envelope returned by an individually resolved single hollow corner-cube retroreflector (HCCR), converted to absolute range and analyzed through its time-dependent mean and covariance. The response occurs at lunar orbital harmonics; the dominant low-eccentricity channel is centered at $f_2=0.847245\,μ{\rm Hz}$, and a five-year broadband forecast applies to spectra smooth over the resolution scale $T_{\rm obs}^{-1}=6.34\,$nHz about that resonance. A scalar 1-kW, 1064-nm link yields $5.893\times10^3$ detected photons s$^{-1}$ and an $88.8$--$124.3\,μ$m photon contribution in 100 s, while the forecasts adopt projected total range precisions of $80$ and $50\,μ$m. In the covariance-dominated weak-signal regime, $Ω_{\rm gw}^{95}\proptoσ_R^2\nuEff^{-1}T_{\rm obs}^{-4}$. Using the published Earth--Moon response normalization, the five-year 95\% thresholds are $1.86\times10^{-7}\Dtot$ for $80\,μ$m and $500\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ and $2.42\times10^{-8}\Dtot$ for $50\,μ$m and $1500\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, where $\Dtot$ is the full-analysis threshold divided by the unit-factor response-anchored forecast. If end-to-end calibration, sampling, and marginalization give $\Dtot\le1.15$, the higher-performance campaign reaches nominal source-statistic equality for $Ω_{\rm gw}=7.08\times10^{-8}$ in five years. These measurable performance and information-retention requirements define high-power AM-CW LLR as a standalone quantitative SGWB experiment at the $0.85\,μ{\rm Hz}$ Earth--Moon resonance.

records.title: In Flight Anthropometry and Health Surveillance for Future Exploration Missions
records.summary: As astronauts are exposed to microgravity the body shape and size change which can affect suit fit, health surveillance, and hardware configurations. Previous studies on the International Space Station (ISS) and Space Shuttle have shown up to 3% stature and 6% sitting height change can occur due to microgravity exposure (Young et al., 2020, 2021). While these studies provided critical data previously unavailable for space exploration, several limitations were also noted for Lunar and Mars Missions. Given the need for high-temporal resolution and future mission relevant anthropometry data which was not fully available in the past in-flight crew anthropometry studies, a new measurement initiative was recently kicked off with NASA. One of the key expansions for the new data collection is incorporating crew medical monitoring components in addition to the traditional focus for suit and hardware fit. This data will be used in conjunction with body mass to determine if there is any correlation between the two sets of data to assist in detecting health and body changes that may occur during future exploration missions where body mass hardware is not available. The timepoints were also adjusted to capture how quickly the changes might occur, changes prior to return to earth, and how quickly crewmembers’ recovery, with an aim to capture both the transient phase and steady-state phases of crew anthropometric changes. This is particularly important as the Lunar Missions involve more frequent gravity changes, such as 1-g to 0-g, then 0-g to 1/6-g. Ideally, this data would be captured using 3d scan technology as in the ground laboratory. However, due to constraints, manual measurements are currently being collected while scan technology is developed. As technology improves and potential hardware is developed that might work on ISS or lunar surface, ground-based efforts continue to collect scan data preflight and postflight. Continued effort has been in progress to identify the optimal technology for in-flight body scanning, which can substantially improve the data resolution matching the ground reference measurements.

records.title: Initiating Cartographic Standards for Artemis III Map Products Used By Crew and Flight Control Team
records.summary: The Artemis missions are reintroducing the need for spatial data products to plan, train, and execute mission objectives for the lunar surface. Spatial data products were used during the Apollo era across the entire mission life cycle, including identification of landing sites, tracking of orbital paths across the lunar surface in Apollo Mission Control, and execution of surface extravehicular activity (EVA) traverses and stations. In the decades since, the transition of NASA’s human spaceflight focus to the Shuttle program and the International Space Station (ISS) has caused the stagnation in use of planetary spatial data beyond the Earth. The most recent spatial data products for crewed lunar activities were created in the 1970’s and have become outdated due to significant advances in lunar dataset volume and diversity, digital geographic information system (GIS) capabilities, and cartographic standards that have evolved to leverage GIS capabilities to answer novel problems. Therefore, the Analysis & Mapping for Planetary Exploration and Science (AMPES) team at NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) is seeking to modernize NASA’s cartographic standards for spatial data products that are specific to surface-scale lunar activities to be responsive to the operational needs of crewed Artemis missions.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Innovation in Preserving and Sharing NASA’s Knowledge
records.summary: Historical knowledge gained from human spaceflight and advances in technology over the last several decades will be the foundation for planning Artemis and Mars missions. Spacesuits, Tools, and Rovers (STAR) Productions is a small, highly skilled, and motivated team helping NASA build a library of knowledge, which will ultimately help facilitate NASA’s missions. Since its inception in 2007, STAR Productions has expanded to meet its customers’ needs. STAR Productions uses their flexibility and creativity to develop more effective ways of harnessing and communicating knowledge. The scope of STAR Productions’ archived knowledge spans from NASA’s infancy to the Artemis Program and currently includes over 280 archived products. This knowledge is shared with NASA scientists, technicians, engineers, vendors, academia, and the public for their use and benefit. Valuable knowledge and lessons are captured in person and virtually of subject matter experts, hardware, facilities, testing, and training, and include mission-related historical documentation. To capture knowledge, the team uses methods such as lectures, workshops, panels, interviews, and educational outreach. Although much of the knowledge captured is technical and aimed at augmenting the space community, there is also a desire to inform the public of NASA’s mission. In 2024, the team released storytelling through “What’s Behind This Door” and Exploring the Moon” series, adding to their repertoire. These series share the what, the why, and the how behind NASA’s current mission internally, as well as through social media. In 2025, “NASA Talks” debuted as a new educational series whereby experts deliver 20-minute lectures. This paper details STAR Productions’ innovation in preserving and sharing NASA’s knowledge.

records.title: Investigation of Spacetime and Its Adequate Coordinate System with Observations by Spacelab and Artemis II
records.summary: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) realized, that General Relativity Theory (GRT) with its hypothetic coordinate systems is insufficient for space flight. The IAU proclaimed the problem of finding an Adequate Coordinate System (ACS). As a provisional solution, the IAU recommended Celestial Reference Systems (CRS). It has been shown that there is an ACS at each point in the universe, and near a celestial body, the ACS is at rest at the celestial body's field. In the Artemis II mission, the spacecraft traveled through a region, in which a superposition of moving fields takes place, originating from Earth, Sun and Moon. Present - day advanced theories about GRT, such as the PPN and PNA, treat only a single CRS in each region. According the superposition problem of moving fields is identified. A deep solution about the physics of space and time is used, in order to solve this problem. The solution is applied to the Artemis II mission.

records.title: Juice-SWI during the Lunar-Earth-Gravity-Assist (LEGA) - Part 2: Instrument operations
records.summary: The Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) embarked in 2023 on a 8-year interplanetary journey to Jupiter and its icy moons. The Submillimetre Wave Instrument (SWI) is one of the ten science instruments aboard the spacecraft. SWI is a sophisticated and first-of-its-kind payload visiting the outer solar system, featuring dual-band tunable receivers, two independent pointing mechanisms, and spectrometers capable of high resolution (up to a resolving power of 10^{7}). It is designed to support the diverse science objectives of the Juice mission targeting Jupiter's middle atmosphere, icy-moon's exospheres as well as near sub-surface thermophysical properties. For this purpose the Juice mission adopts a complex trajectory tour within the Jovian system, which further necessitates a sophisticated, mission-driven operations concept for SWI. This presents significant planning, operations and commanding challenges which are described in this paper in the context of the Lunar and Earth Gravity Assist (LEGA). After the development and ground calibration of the instrument, the SWI Team has designed a comprehensive calibration strategy applicable during the Cruise Phase of Juice. Among the various opportunities for calibration, including the Near-Earth Commissioning Phase and more than ten Payload Checkout Windows, the LEGA offers the means not only to improve the calibration of the instrument, but also to validate the operational strategy of future icy moon flybys.

records.title: Low-Thrust Trajectory Optimization for Cubesat Lunar Mission: HORYU-VI
records.summary: A three-stage low-thrust trajectory is investigated for the HORYU-VI CubeSat lunar mission: pre-flyby deceleration, lunar capture, and orbit circularization. Impulsive reference trajectories initialize finite-burn targeting in the General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). The archived case uses constant 12 kg spacecraft mass and 1.08 mN effective thrust. The first reported bound lunar state occurs at day 184.1. At the end of the 381.3-day record, the osculating lunar orbit has semi-major axis 3,862 km and eccentricity 0.0867. Integrating the reported thrust state yields an estimated velocity increment of 839.8 m/s over 108.00 days of thrust. At the configured 2800 s specific impulse, the ideal rocket-equation propellant equivalent is 0.361 kg; mass depletion was disabled in the propagation. The record demonstrates lunar capture and partial circularization. Completion of the intended 100 km science orbit, coupled mass-depleting propagation, and uncertainty analysis remain necessary to assess operational feasibility.

records.title: Lunar base agent-based modeling - A benchmark for simulating crewed space missions
records.summary: Space exploration has progressed significantly since the mid-20th century, and recent technological advancements, along with the emergence of commercial space travel, have led to substantial leaps in planning for future space missions. The largest planned upcoming mission is the Artemis program, supported by NASA and the international Artemis Accords, which aims to create the first permanent human presence on the Moon and in deep space (the Moon to Mars architecture). Although human psychology and team science have been crucial for the success of past space missions, from the Apollo program and Skylab to the Space Shuttle (STS) and the International Space Station (ISS), human factors and social behavior will become even more ubiquitous and essential for space missions in the new era of commercial space. By simulating upcoming permanent space missions in an agent-based model (ABM), we can draw insights into the long-term effects of human factors and interactions in space. Drawing from the literature on proxy environments (extreme environments on Earth (i.e., Antarctica), space analogs, and past space missions), and on theories of small group complex systems and team science, we created a highly probable representation or simulation of expected social interactions between astronauts, and astronauts with the lunar environment for the Artemis program (i.e., Artemis IV (Lunar Gateway) and Artemis V (Lunar South Pole Base)). Our Lunar Base ABM explores the exogenous and endogenous factors that are more likely to lead to sustainable versus catastrophic scenarios on the Moon in the next couple of decades. The model represents astronauts using a new Agent_Astronaut framework with cognitive skills, emotional states, and personality traits to capture how social and environmental factors interact to affect mission outcomes. Monte Carlo simulations consisting of tens of thousands of iterations show trade-offs in productivity and psychological well-being. This approach demonstrates how agent-based modeling can help mission planners evaluate operational resilience, team structures, and workload dynamics in support of future lunar exploration.

records.title: Lunar Glovebox Development
records.summary: This effort will identify technologies in current, operational gloveboxes that can be upgraded. Targeted improvements will be efficiency, sound levels, and power consumption. Additional goals will be to reduce the overall complexity, and thereby the system requirements, while maintaining essential safety and performance. This will improve reliability and ensure levels of containment remain if a system fails. Benefits: A glovebox system with reduced complexity and improved efficiency. This will enable operation across a broader range of vehicles while allowing users to conduct activities in an isolated, dust-free volume.

records.title: Lunar Orbit Evolution and Strategies for Planetary Protection
records.summary: * To support planetary protection (PP) compliance and sustainable lunar exploration, we investigate the natural dynamical behavior of low lunar orbits (LLOs) as a mechanism for predictable disposal, contamination risk reduction, and stable staging architectures. * Under the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR) planetary protection framework, Moon missions are classified as Category II, IIa, and IIb, requiring assessment and documentation of impact locations and forward-contamination pathways. Predictable orbital decay and long-term stability are therefore critical for end-of-mission design. * We analyze families of LLOs spanning ~10–250 km altitude and 80°–100° inclination (i.e., polar and near-polar) representative of pre- and post-descent staging orbits for NASA’s Artemis Human Landing System (HLS) program and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) Initiative missions. * High-fidelity propagations via flight-proven astrodynamics software (STK and GMAT) reveal two dominant behaviors. 1) Naturally decaying trajectories produce deterministic surface impacts that cluster into geographically confined latitude–longitude corridors governed primarily by initial orbital geometry. 2) Frozen and quasi-stable regimes exhibit multi-year to decadal lifetimes with negligible impact likelihood, forming candidate “graveyard” or staging orbits.
keywords: Planetary Protection Policy at the Moon

records.title: LunarDepthNet: Generation of Digital Elevation Models using Deep Learning and Monocular Satellite Images
records.summary: Recent times have seen an increase in demand of high quality Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the lunar surface, because they are highly important for studying the moon and planning future missions. However, there is an evident lack of detailed elevation data on the Moon. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel deep learning method that estimates and generates a surface elevation map directly from monocular images of the surface. The dataset used comprises of the Chandrayaan-2 Terrain Mapping Camera (TMC) images with their corresponding Digital Terrain Models (DTMs). The study proposes LunarDepthNet, which comprises of a UNet architecture to generate DEMS. It incorporates an EfficientNet encoder and custom layers to correctly learn how the light shadows on the surface relate to the actual elevation values. A combined loss function was also utilized to keep the terrain details accurate and smooth. During validation, the model showed a stable loss convergence of 12%. It achieved a mean nRMSE of 0.437 and an MAE of 4.5m in the testing stage. These results prove the model can generate dependable elevation maps from single orbital images, which are quite useful in regions of the moon where stereo-images are not available.

records.title: Mauna: Automating High Throughput Orbit Propagation for NASA Missions
records.summary: What is MAUNA? MAUNA automates high-throughput spacecraft trajectory analysis by generating, executing, and post-processing thousands of General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) propagations across multidimensional design spaces. This replaces manually created and modified scripts with a standardized, reproducible workflow and enables systematic exploration of large orbital trade spaces. Where does AI/ML actually enter? Mauna-generated high-fidelity trajectory data provide a foundation for physics-informed machine learning. For lunar impact prediction, machine learning (ML) can learn the slow, long-term evolution of orbital states while known gravitational physics constrain the solution; trajectories are then returned to high-fidelity numerical propagation near the terminal event to accurately resolve the impact location. What has NASA actually used this for / why does it matter? The framework has been applied to lunar mission-design problems supporting NASA’s Artemis HLS and CLPS programs, including high-fidelity low-lunar-orbit stability analysis, automated searches across hundreds of thousands of candidate trajectories, and mapping of natural impact/disposal behavior. This combination of automation, physics-based simulation, and ML enables faster identification of stable orbital regimes and potential surface-interaction risks.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Model Correlation and Thermal Analysis of xEMU Boot at Lunar South Pole Temperatures
records.summary: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Artemis program plans to send astronauts to the lunar south pole, a region of the moon that is colder than previous lunar missions and low earth orbit operations. The spacesuit boots that will be used on these missions will be directly impacted by these extremely cold temperatures (down to ~50 K). To assess the performance of the Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU) lunar boot in these extreme temperatures, the boot was tested at the Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) in the Cryogenic Ice Transfer, Acquisition Development, and Excavation Laboratory (CITADEL) thermal vacuum (TVAC) chamber. This data was used to correlate thermal models to predict operational performance of the boots on the lunar south pole. This paper documents the data analysis, thermal boot model correlation, and operational predictions conducted using data from the xEMU TVAC test. Data from the test series was used to determine expected thermal conductances within the boot and between the boot and environment. These conductances were used to correlate a Thermal Desktop model of the xEMU boot across 10 different test points which varied external temperature, internal boot ventilation flowrate, and contact pressure. The correlated model was then used to predict operational performance in the lunar south pole. While the predictions indicate promising evidence for performance of the boots at the 100K test point, there is still substantial uncertainty in performance, particularly at the 48K test point. The results of this test series and model correlation stress the importance of improved testing for characterizing the expected thermal resistance between the outside of the boot and the lunar surface.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Moon Base Transportation - Deliveries to the Lunar Surface
records.summary: Development of the Moon Base will enable a home away from home for astronauts who will live and work at humanity’s first lunar outpost. In this effort, NASA’s Moon Transportation Office is responsible for enabling the transformational missions required to deliver habitats, supplies, science payloads, and all other elements needed to cultivate a permanent presence on the Lunar Surface. The Mission Concept (MC) is characterized through evaluation of an end-to-end architecture that can successfully deliver a generalized heavy large-volume payload, in excess of 4000 kg, to a precision landing and touchdown on the lunar surface. The mission architecture utilizes a single launch configuration of a Lunar Lander (LL) with a unique propellant system. The LL has an integral orbital transfer capability and features jettisonable elements. The design circumvents the need for prop transfer on orbit and multiple launch configurations. The launch vehicle (LV) for this work will assume the capability to deliver a payload in excess of 40,000 kg to orbit, affording multiple LV solutions. Considerations for the LL and payload deployment from the fairing are assumed to be handled through compliance with a launch providers’ Interface Requirements Document (IRD). The MC will span from launch at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) to terminal descent and touchdown on the lunar surface, requiring a total ΔV on the order of 6 km/s beyond what is required to get the vehicle stack to a 200 km circular Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Major mission phases include: launch and launch vehicle separation, transfer operations, pre-landing navigation, and lunar descent and touchdown. A Concept of Operations (ConOps) is used as the primary design driver for defining architecture of the vehicles necessary to achieve final payload delivery. Numerous ground rules and assumptions will be provided for each phase of the mission. Concept designs for the LL is presented. An emphasis of the design maximizes a feasible path for maturation, manufacturing, and operation. A self-imposed practical consideration for this effort is the incorporation of legacy designed hardware to minimize expensive, time-intensive, and high-risk hardware development cycles. The propulsion system of the LL adopts a conventional storable bipropellant configuration of monomethyl hydrazine (MMH) and mixed oxides of nitrogen (MON3). This effort will showcase a unique propellant delivery system to minimize the reliance on propellant management devices (PMDs) during descent. Numerous key constraints have been considered, across the multiple segments of the mission. These include the unique aspects of center of gravity (CG) management, thruster plume effects including self-impingement, propulsion system hardware limitations, navigation during multiple mission phases, and landing gear geometry for uneven terrain. These constraints shape the trades necessary for precision landing of heavy cargo and ensure compatibility with broader Moon Base ...

records.title: Moon to Mars: Contributions of Optical Measurements to NASA's Artemis Program
records.summary: NASA and partners have embarked on a series of space missions to the moon and Mars, collectively known as the Artemis Program. This talk overviews the Artemis missions and details laser and optical measurement technique development and application to ground and flight tests related to, or inspired by, the Artemis program. Three measurement techniques have been applied to study vehicle launch, Earth and Mars entry, and lunar landing. Such optical instrumentation provides unique information to inform the underlying physics of space flight while also providing benchmark data for validating ever advancing predictive codes.

records.title: Moonstone: A Multimodal Foundation Model and Benchmark for Lunar Remote Sensing
records.summary: Decades of orbital missions have produced multi-modal remote sensing data for the Moon, spanning optical imagery, spectroscopy, thermal emission, radar, gravity, and elemental composition. Yet these datasets remain fragmented across archives, and no benchmark exists for evaluating machine learning on lunar data. We introduce Moonstone, the first multi-modal foundation model benchmark for lunar remote sensing. Our contributions are: (1) a 28-channel, 128 pixels-per-degree (~237 m) global lunar pretraining dataset from seven instrument families across five missions, (2) MG-MAE, a modality-grouped masked autoencoder with per-group convolutional tokenizers, a shared Vision Transformer encoder, attention masking for missing modalities, coverage-adaptive masking for heterogeneous spatial coverage, and spectral continuity regularization for physically plausible reconstructions, and (3) a benchmark of six downstream tasks covering classification, regression, and segmentation. MG-MAE pretrained features outperform scratch baselines on all tasks and surpass both ImageNet-pretrained and vanilla MAE baselines by large margins. Data and code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ayushprd/Moonstone and https://github.com/ayushprd/Moonstone .

records.title: MSolo for Commercial Partnerships
records.summary: MSolo is a modified commercial off the shelf (COTS) instrument based on a gas analyzer from INFICON, a company marketing to the semiconductor and vacuum coating industries, security and energy industries, and automotive and refrigeration industries. The unit is highly automated, provides fast-scan capabilities with high sensitivity as demanded by terrestrial end-users, and is now ruggedized for spaceflight. The COTS instrument was tested in various space environments and both structural and electrical modifications were made to improve the instrument’s performance, robustness, and spaceflight readiness. The instrument successfully operated on the lunar surface during the Intuitive Machine – 2 Mission. Gas analysis is a critical tool for science investigations, resource characterization, and for characterization of ISRU processes. Numerous future mission needs for gas analysis already exist. Today there are multiple commercial companies working on a developing ISRU and prospecting mission concepts, with several of these prospecting mission concepts and process development testbeds currently using the commercially available version of the MSolo instrument. The ability to modify the commercial version of the mass spectrometer for spaceflight allows for projects to use the commercial units, which are low-cost high fidelity test unit, that can be integrated into a low TRL mission concepts as engineering development units, enabling the government and commercial programs to focus on the improving ISRU process without needing to develop a high-fidelity gas analysis method. MSolo is a unique solution, providing hardware that maintains functionality regardless of its application. In addition to MSolo opportunities, Interlune will build on their successful Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase 1 to perform technology maturation of the key technology demonstration elements of the Prospect Moon payload. Maturing this technology to the point of flight readiness will position this commercial team to be ready for integration into a lunar lander as a part of a future flight opportunity. Prospect Moon will demonstrate a number of commercial technologies relevant to lunar resources and generate relevant data for future Artemis program use Benefits: NASA’s investment in MSolo has resulted in a flight-ready, modular, and highly adaptable instrument able to be integrated with a wide variety of lander and/or rover designs. The MSolo software has already been adapted to interface with four different Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) providers, showcasing its flexibility and readiness for commercial use. The instrument’s architecture, which includes a SHREC-based hybrid computer and a calibration gas system, supports in-situ calibration and real-time volatile analysis, making it a valuable asset for both scientific investigations and ...

records.title: NASA's LEIA Mission: Investigating the Biological Response to the Lunar Surface Environment
records.summary: The Lunar Explorer Instrument for space biology Applications (LEIA) mission will investigate the effects of the lunar environment (partial gravity and space radiation) on biological organisms, particularly the effects on DNA damage repair and stress response and on synthetic biomanufacturing of dietary antioxidants. LEIA will launch no earlier than October 2027 as a payload on an Intuitive Machines lunar lander. LEIA is science suite of three instruments: a microfluidic-based system or BioSensor with life support capabilities, a charged particle detector (LET spectrometer), and a mini fast neutron detector (mini-FND). The BioSensor instrument has high heritage from NASA’s BioSentinel CubeSat mission, which was launched to a heliocentric orbit onboard the Artemis I rocket in late 2022 (currently at ~100 million kms from the Earth). A similar payload performed experiments on the International Space Station (ISS) in 2022. The BioSensor instrument contains a complex fluidic system that delivers nutrients to desiccated yeast cells in fluidic cards. Growth and metabolic activity are then monitored via optical measurements, which allows for detection of changes caused by cellular or DNA damage after exposure to the lunar surface environment, as well as bio production of antioxidants as a potential countermeasure for future manned missions to the Moon. The LET spectrometer and mini-FND instruments will quantify and characterize the lunar surface radiation environment. Lessons learned from BioSentinel have been implemented in the design and development of LEIA. LEIA is supported by NASA’s Exploration Science Strategy and Integration Office (ESSIO) in the Science Mission Directorate (SMD).
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems: Development and Demonstration of Technologies Enabling Swarms and New Spacecraft Platforms with AI and Edge Computing
records.summary: NASA’s Small Spacecraft & Distributed Systems (SSDS) within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate (RTMD) expands U.S. capability to execute unique missions through targeted investment, rapid development, and flight demonstration of small spacecraft technologies applicable to exploration, science and the commercial space sector. SSDS strategically invests in technology development and on-orbit demonstrations executed across NASA, other government agencies, industry, and academia. The program’s University SmallSat Technology Partnerships initiative awards academic researchers with the opportunity to collaborate with NASA to mature innovative technology. Capabilities aligned with RTMD’s technology shortfalls and interests - power, processing, propulsion, sensors, communications, autonomous navigation, architectures, and advanced applications like artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and edge computing - are prioritized in SSDS investments. These investments enable distributed, autonomous, and cooperative small spacecraft systems that support swarm missions extending beyond low Earth orbit into cislunar and deep space. This paper highlights representative SSDS flight demonstrations that mature these capabilities to enable a future operational infrastructure needed to support sustained exploration of the Moon and beyond. SSDS’s investment strategy emphasizes rapid development and on-orbit demonstration to validate spacecraft technologies required for swarms and distributed mission architectures. The Starling swarm technology demonstration mission exemplifies this approach by advancing distributed spacecraft autonomy, cooperative operations, and space situational awareness. Extended flight testing and ongoing studies of next generation swarm configurations and on-orbit space traffic monitoring and management continue to inform future swarm designs. DiskSat’s four-spacecraft demonstration mission represents SSDS’s strategic vision to expand the design space for future small spacecraft through its commitment to advance novel platform concepts that can impact how science is performed on orbit. Continuing to invest in future platforms, the notional PY12 concept is a 12-spacecraft swarm hosting neuromorphic processors and is envisioned as an on-orbit testbed for AI, edge computing, and positioning, navigation and timing technologies. SSDS also invests in single-spacecraft technology demonstrations that underpin the success of future swarm missions and accelerate the availability of validated technologies across the small spacecraft ecosystem. Examples of such demonstrations include Pathfinder Technology Demonstrator-3 (PTD-3), which performed high-rate optical communications; PTD-R, which demonstrated a camera capable of simultaneous ultraviolet and short-wave infrared optical sensing; and CAPSTONE, the Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology and Operations Navigation Experiment, which validated autonomous navigation in ...

records.title: NASA’s Artemis II Test Flight: Lessons Learned
records.summary: Through Artemis, NASA, along with its industrial and international partners, is undertaking an increasingly complex series of test flights to return humans to the Moon with the goal of constructing a Moon Base and establishing a sustainable, enduring presence on the surface to prepare for the human exploration of Mars. As the bridge between the Artemis I uncrewed test flight and additional test flights that will enable enduring human exploration of the lunar surface, the Artemis II mission – the first crewed flight under Artemis – provided critical human-in-the-loop operational and scientific data. This paper provides an overview of some of the major outcomes of the Artemis II test flight, from the in-flight performance and handling of NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion spacecraft to groundcrew operations and dedicated scientific investigations. During the nearly 10-day mission, the crew, which included three NASA astronauts and one Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut, conducted manual and automated spacecraft operations; monitored and evaluated Orion’s life-support, propulsion, power, thermal, communication, and navigation systems; performed a proximity operations demonstration; and, assessed habitability and crew interfaces. Artemis II demonstrated an essential balance between crew decision-making and ground support that builds on decades of human spaceflight experience. The analysis of this flight is feeding forward into future Artemis missions. Mission control, including the new Orion Mission Evaluation Room and Science Evaluation Room, played a critical role in monitoring and controlling systems, providing analysis and support for crew decision making. The systems tested during Artemis II also inform how the crew and ground teams can effectively and efficiently work together during human exploration of the lunar South Pole under Artemis.

records.title: Nonspherical Silica Nanoparticle Aggregates Exacerbate Pulmonary Surfactant Monolayer Disturbance
records.summary: To enhance understanding of the biotoxicity of inhaled lunar dust (LD) and safeguard astronaut health during future crewed lunar missions, we performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of nine silica nanoparticle (SiNP) aggregates─the primary component of LD─varying in size (3 and 6 nm), shape (sphere, ellipsoid, and cube), and surface features (0, 1, and 3 bulges) interacting with a pulmonary surfactant (PS) monolayer. The key findings are (1) shape, not size, governs aggregate architecture and fate: cubic SiNPs yield the most aspherical, rapidly forming aggregates and switch translocation from penetration to embedding when present as 6 nm members, and aggregation time scales as cube > ellipsoid > sphere. (2) Aggregates induce greater PS disturbance than equal-volume single SiNP, and the DPPC order parameter S z falls to 0.678-0.706 and is driven lower (0.587-0.720) when nonspherical SiNPs dominate the aggregates. (3) Surface bulges normally hinder translocation, yet once their size and number exceed a threshold, they locally rupture the PS monolayer and shorten translocation while still increasing PS adsorption and S z . These findings establish that aggregate morphology, rather than mass, exacerbates PS monolayer disturbance and provide quantitative benchmarks for guiding dust-mitigation strategies for future lunar missions.

records.title: Organic Inventory - Planetary Protection on the Moon
records.summary: All spacecraft generate and carry contaminants, i.e., unwanted and potentially harmful material. When a spacecraft lands and operates in vacuum, as onto Earth’s Moon, it introduces contaminants into its environment that may compromise mission science objectives and engineering performance. Contamination may degrade sites of unique value to planetary science or in situ resource utilization. This presentation will identify and compare source terms and transport vectors for contaminants – in particular, organic material – generated by landed spacecraft. An integrated modeling framework for the organic contamination footprint of spacecraft missions will be described and presented.

records.title: Physical characterization of Earth's quasi-satellite 2025 PN7
records.summary: A hypothetical origin as lunar ejecta for Earth's quasi-satellites (QS) has gained initial support in recent years, but there is scarce photometric and/or spectroscopic data to support the premise due to the rare observational windows to obtain such data for these small objects. One of the key pieces of evidence supporting the lunar-origin hypothesis, the lunar-like, very red reflectance spectrum of QS (469219) Kamo'oalewa, was recently found to be flawed. We present reflectance spectroscopy of Earth's QS 2025~PN$_7$ obtained with FORS2 at UT1-Antu of the ESO Very Large Telescope. This is only the second QS that has ever been characterized, the first being (469219) Kamo'oalewa, the sample-return target of the Tianwen-2 mission. Our results indicate that 2025~PN$_7$ exhibits a near-solar, flat visual spectrum, most consistent with the B-type in the Bus-DeMeo taxonomy. Our results therefore still support an asteroid-belt origin for most of Earth's QSs. The lunar-ejecta hypothesis can only be formally rejected with a larger sample of spectroscopically characterized QSs.

records.title: Planetary Protection Compliance of NASA Missions – Past, Present and Future
records.summary: NASA monitors its spacecraft from a planetary protection (PP) perspective, to ensure continued compliance with planetary protection requirements. This report to COSPAR on previous, ongoing and future missions will describe the issues and considerations regarding the PP implementation and compliance status of each mission, with changes noted as appropriate from previous reports. Missions not described in other presentations will be covered, including (but not limited to): Europa Clipper, Juno, Curiosity, Perseverance, Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE), Dragonfly, Artemis II, and Artemis III.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Post-Flight Assessment of the OSIRIS-REx Sample Return Capsule (SRC) for Organic and Other Potential Contaminants
records.summary: Regolith samples from the carbonaceous asteroid Bennu were stowed and delivered to Earth in the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft’s Sample Return Capsule (SRC). We applied multiple analytical techniques to study the components of the post-flight SRC, with a focus on assessing the conditions and any contaminants to which the Bennu samples were exposed. Examination of the passive temperature sensors placed inside the SRC, in combination with thermal modeling results, indicates that the samples were not heated above the 75°C limit imposed by OSIRIS-REx mission requirements. The sample canister air filter was found to contain Bennu particulates that had escaped from the sample collector, as well as a range of contaminants likely associated with the original filter component materials. No indications of terrestrial soils were found in the filter. Isotopic analyses of organic compounds and noble gases trapped in the filter show values consistent with terrestrial origins, and there are no indications of trapped asteroidal volatiles. Organic compounds found in the flight filter that were not present in a non-flight control filter include aromatic hydrocarbons, alkylated aromatic hydrocarbons, phenolic-related compounds, aliphatic hydrocarbons, and alcohols. The abundances of these organic compounds typically decrease from outer layers of the filter towards the canister interior, suggesting that they are external contaminants. We conclude that the majority of these organic compounds are chemical byproducts associated with outgassing of the SRC heatshield and backshell following the ablation portion of SRC atmospheric entry. Overall, our findings show that the OSIRIS-REx SRC performed excellently in containerizing the asteroidal samples obtained at Bennu, delivering them safely to the ground at the UTTR, and preventing most, though perhaps not all, external contaminants from reaching them. We discuss lessons learned from the flight and recovery of the OSIRIS-REx SRC that can benefit future sample return missions.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Powering the Lunar Surface: Managing Dust, Extreme Environments, and Power Needs
records.summary: Power availability remains one of the primary constraints for lunar surface science. This talk reviews power requirements from previously flown instruments to help prepare future payloads for upcoming CLPS opportunities and highlights the testing and environmental simulation capabilities at NASA JSC that enable reliable lunar payload development. It also outlines the power needs, environmental challenges, and emerging technologies required to support sustained human and robotic operations on the lunar surface as part of NASA’s Moon to Mars strategy. Key challenges include variable solar illumination at polar and equatorial regions, extreme thermal environments, and dust driven degradation that limit current surface power systems. The science data needed for resource identification and landing site planning will allow for the successful preparation of crewed Artemis activities and long-term presence. Building on recent missions, current test infrastructure, and emerging power technology pathways, this presentation equips industry, academia, and government teams with the information needed to design robust lunar payloads, reduce development risk, and fully leverage the increasing cadence of CLPS missions. These developments will form a critical technical foundation for long duration lunar presence and future Mars exploration.

records.title: Quantum Technology Advice and Guidance
records.summary: The purpose of this role is to serve as the strategic lead for integrating emerging quantum technologies into STMD’s Enable program, specifically supporting Advanced Avionics and Sensors and Materials, Structures, and Manufacturing. As NASA prioritizes Moon-to-Mars, technologies that provide unprecedented precision and autonomy are critical, of which quantum technologies may offer extraordinary quantum advantage. This role will centralize knowledge of quantum investments across the agency, assess their maturity, and guide STMD’s Enable program future investment strategy to bridge the gap between laboratory research and flight-ready demonstrations for deep space exploration. The Quantum Technology Advisor will execute the following primary tasks: • Cross-Center Quantum Inventory: Actively survey and collect data on current and planned quantum technology research and investments across all NASA centers. • Technology Mapping & Alignment: Analyze the collected data to determine how these quantum technologies map to STMD’s Enable program Avionics and Sensors initiatives. • Strategic Recommendations: Evaluate the cross-center portfolio and formulate strategic recommendations for future STMD Enable program investments. Recommendations must emphasize technologies that directly enable Moon-to-Mars objectives. The Quantum Technology Advisor will be expected to deliver the following to STMD’s Enable program leadership: • Quarterly Status Briefings: Brief updates detailing the progress of cross-center data collection and emerging trends. • NASA Quantum Landscape Matrix: A consolidated database/matrix cataloging all identified quantum projects across NASA centers, including their current TRL, primary applications, and lead center. • Draft Investment Strategy Report: A preliminary document outlining high-potential quantum technologies that warrant STMD investment, specifically highlighting their impact on Moon to Mars avionics and sensor goals. • Final Executive Briefing & Report: A comprehensive final presentation and written report summarizing the cross-center findings and detailing prioritized, actionable investment recommendations for the STMD Enable program.
